newsitem.title: UK: Significant copper tonnage is off-market now.
newsitem.headline: Significant copper tonnage is off-market now.

text.p: A declining proportion of copper stocks are registered in Western exchange warehouses and these may account now for only one-third of the global copper surplus, industry analysts Bloomsbury Minerals Economics (BME) said.

In a special briefing, BME said the Chinese Strategic Reserve Board (SRB) is understood to have stocks double those on the London Metal Exchange (LME). Meanwhile, South East Asian consumer stocks are said to be more than double those on Comex.
Also, the World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS) reported on Wednesday the possibility of nearly 600,000 tonnes of non-LME copper in Netherlands bonded warehouses.
This is in contrast to the late 1980s, when almost all surplus copper was on the exchanges.
"If there are "hidden' stockpiles perhaps the big players in the market are more aware of them now then they were three years ago," BME said.
BME figures show that copper surplus to trade requirements divides in the following way --
- LME and Comex stocks total approximately 150,000 tonnes.
- Chinese bonded warehouses or transit material acccount for 250,000 tonnes.
- South East Asian consigment inventory is pegged around 50,000 tonnes.
Although headline exchange stocks are low (LME inventory is the lowest since September 1990) copper prices have underperformed recently, some market traders said.
Since the June 1996 shakeout after the Sumitomo Corp scandal, prices have languished even though since September there has been a 166,600-tonne or 60 percent fall in LME stocks.
"Exchange prices seem now to be responding to the total picture rather than to just the level of stocks," BME said.
